author: Kelly Sullivan Special to The Sun
title: Country Road Chronicles: Young housewife claimed mop attack | Guest Columns | thewesterlysun.com
text:
A lone mop was propped up against an interior wall of the Third District courthouse on the morning of Aug. 1, 1924. According to 26-year-old Hope Valley housewife Madeline Baton, the cleaning tool was the weapon used by neighbor Julia Vincent to brutally assault her.
Madeline resided on Main Street with her husband Clarence Eugene Baton and their five children, the oldest being nine-year-old Clarence and the youngest being 14-month-old Erlo. On the same street lived John Vincent, a native of Canada and an employee of a local mill, and his 31-year-old wife Julia, a native of Belgium. Many other residents of the area were of Polish descent – Andrew Zegarzewsky, Mary Jakyowski, Tony Dobroski, and Mary Pukas among them.
That summer of 1924, Julia’s 13-year-old daughter Engletine was allegedly crossing through the yard of the Batons’ property when Madeline took issue with the trespass. Soon after the event, an angry Julia arrived at Madeline’s house, accusing her of slapping Engletine. A loud argument between the two women ensued and Julia later described Madeline eventually turning and going into her house, then coming back out moments later with a mop in her hands.
In court, Julia testified that she was afraid Madeline intended to hit her with the mop so reached out to grab it. According to Julia, the mop snapped in half when she did so. This testimony did not match that of Madeline, who took the stand to tell the court how Julia grabbed the mop out of her hands and struck her over the head with it. She stated that the resulting injury required medical attention.
Following the ugly meet-up at the Baton home, Madeline made a formal complaint to authorities and Julia was arrested and charged with violent assault. She pleaded not guilty and was presented with a bail of $500.
Those who witnessed the confrontation on Main Street were unable to speak English. Thirteen-year-old Fred Dobroski, who had come to Hope Valley from New Bedford, Mass. to visit Tony Dobroski and his family, luckily knew enough English that he was able to serve as a translator in court. Each time an attorney asked a question in English, he would repeat it in Polish to whatever witness of West Slavic ethnicity was on the stand. When the witness answered, he would repeat the testimony in English for the benefit of the attorneys, the judge, and those in the courtroom.
No documentation has been located concerning the outcome of the case. In addition, the Vincent family does not seem to have any presence within Rhode Island after the year 1925, indicating they may have relocated to another state or even internationally.
The Batons remained living in the areas of Hopkinton and Richmond for the rest of their lives, save for the years Madeline resided in a Westerly nursing home. If the assault she claimed to have undergone at the hands of Julia Vincent actually occurred, it did not have long-term physical consequences. Madeline went on to have five more children, and died on Jan. 18, 1990 at the age of 92.
Kelly Sullivan is a journalist and author who lives in Hope Valley. You can contact her at kjshem77@gmail.com.
